content_html_sanitized:
Posted April 19, 2002

I just spoke to Steve Kubby. He is back with his family. He sounded very weak, but in his typically good spirit, determined to keep speaking truth to power.
See

This has been a truly bizarre week. I am in San Francisco for the NORML conference, which is probably the largest and best ever. In the meantime, my friends in Vancouver have been subjected to pointlessly inhumane abuse by the Canadian police and immigration system.

Of course, the great BC lawyer, John Conroy -- who represented Renee Boje, is also here for the NORML conference. Consequently, we have been working long distance trying to help the immigration lawyer retained by Marc Emery. As I said last night, Marc's generosity undoubtedly saved their lives.

Fortunately, Steve Tuck was released yesterday afternoon, but the Kubby situation became really bizarre last night. First, I was told in the afternoon that Kubby's release was imminent, and heard nothing to the contrary, so I reported his release. Then late in the day, Michele Kubby called greatly relieved and told me that Steve's was being released. Then, late last night I learned that he still had not been released. Apparently, Canadian immigration decided to reinstate their charges, although this has not been confirmed. This required that he be held overnight.

At that point Steve's medical condition was going from very painful to life-threatening, but there was another hearing this afternoon, and he was finally released.

Unfortunately, Canadian immigration decided today to arrest Ken Hayes, who was indicted in the California medical cannabis case involving Ed Rosenthal. We had hoped that they would not hassle Ken, having just arrested and released him a few weeks ago. Because they waited until Friday to arrest Hayes, this means that he will be held over the weekend, but he will be moved to another facility, where he will be treated much better than Kubby and Tuck. There will be a hearing on his case early next week, and I will report the results.

The Canadian immigration department was undoubtedly pushed by DEAland and its Canadian collaborators into acting. However, there can be no excuse for the abusive treatment of two seriously ill Americans -- in violation of Canadian law.

While Canada is far better than DEAland, we should have no illusions about the situation there. Certainly, DEAland pressures play a role, but we should not forget that Canada had national cannabis prohibition before DEAland and its origins were every bit as evil as in DEAland.

See

And there are certainly narks in Canada who are prohibitionist true-believers.
See

The struggle for freedom is global, and there is no refuge from our moral obligation to fight " all forms of tyranny over the mind of man. "
